roles.title: Automation Test Engineer
roles.overview: An Automation Test Engineer turns repeatable test cases into reliable automated checks, typically at the UI and API levels. The role involves choosing what to automate, writing maintainable test code, running it in CI and analysing failures. It is the most common next step for manual testers who learn to program.
responsibilities: Identify test cases that give the best return when automated
Write and maintain automated UI and API tests using an established framework
Run automated suites in CI and triage failures
Keep tests stable by fixing locators, waits and test data issues
Report automation coverage and results to the team
Work with manual testers to keep automated and manual coverage aligned

essential: One programming language (Java, Python, JavaScript or TypeScript)
A UI automation tool such as Selenium or Playwright
A test runner such as TestNG, JUnit or pytest
optional: API automation with REST Assured or a similar library

prerequisites: Basic programming knowledge: variables, conditionals, loops and functions

beginner.title: Programming and first scripts
goals: Write small programs using classes, collections and exceptions
Automate a login test with stable locators
Use explicit waits instead of fixed sleeps
Commit test code to a Git repository

intermediate.title: Maintainable suites
goals: Structure tests with the Page Object Model
Organise tests and assertions with a test runner
Parameterise tests with external data
Build the project with Maven

advanced.title: Automation in delivery
goals: Run the suite in CI on every pull request
Execute tests in parallel safely
Diagnose and fix flaky tests with evidence

exercises: Automate five scenarios on a practice e-commerce site using page objects
Replace every Thread.sleep in a sample suite with appropriate explicit waits
Make a test data-driven from a CSV file and add negative cases
Configure a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the suite and publishes a report

sampleProject.title: UI and API automation suite for a demo store
sampleProject.description: Build a Java or TypeScript project that automates key journeys of a practice e-commerce site using page objects, plus a few API checks for the same features. Include data-driven tests, an HTML report, parallel execution and a CI workflow, with a README explaining design choices and how to run it.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you decide which test cases to automate?
interviewQuestions.a: I prioritise tests that run frequently, cover high-risk or business-critical paths, have stable requirements and deterministic expected results. I avoid automating tests that change constantly, need human judgement such as visual aesthetics, or would cost more to maintain than they save. Where possible I automate at the API level because it is faster and more stable than UI.

interviewQuestions.q: What is the difference between implicit and explicit waits in Selenium?
interviewQuestions.a: An implicit wait sets a global timeout for finding elements, applied to every lookup. An explicit wait waits for a specific condition, such as an element being clickable, for a specific element. Explicit waits are more precise, and mixing the two can produce unpredictable wait times, so I generally use explicit waits only.

interviewQuestions.q: Explain the Page Object Model and its benefits.
interviewQuestions.a: Each page or component is represented by a class that holds its locators and exposes methods for user actions, such as login(user, password). Tests call these methods instead of using locators directly. When the UI changes, only the page object needs updating, which reduces duplication and makes tests readable.

interviewQuestions.q: Your suite passes locally but fails in CI. How do you investigate?
interviewQuestions.a: I compare environments: browser and driver versions, headless mode, screen size, timing, test data and configuration. I review CI artefacts like screenshots, logs and traces from the failure. Common causes are timing differences, missing test data and tests that depend on execution order.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you choose a locator?
interviewQuestions.a: I prefer stable, unique attributes such as dedicated test IDs, then accessible names or IDs, and use CSS selectors over long XPath where possible. I avoid locators tied to layout or generated class names. If no good locator exists, I ask developers to add a test attribute.

roles.codingRequirements: Working proficiency in one language (Java, Python or TypeScript): OOP basics, collections, exceptions, and reading stack traces.
commonMistakes: Claiming automation should replace all manual testing
Using fixed sleeps and calling it synchronisation
Unable to explain the design of your own framework
Focusing only on tool syntax rather than what is worth automating
readinessCriteria: You have a public repository with at least 15 automated tests using page objects
Your suite runs in CI and you can show a passing run
You can write a new test for an unfamiliar page within 30 minutes
You can explain and fix at least two causes of flaky tests

roles.title: Selenium Automation Engineer
roles.overview: A Selenium Automation Engineer specialises in browser automation with Selenium WebDriver, most often in Java with TestNG or JUnit and Maven. Many enterprise teams have large existing Selenium suites, so the role involves deep knowledge of the WebDriver protocol, synchronisation, Selenium Grid and keeping large suites maintainable. The title is tool-specific, but strong fundamentals transfer to other tools.
responsibilities: Develop and maintain Selenium WebDriver tests for web applications
Handle complex UI elements including frames, windows, alerts and dynamic content
Run tests across browsers using Selenium Grid or a cloud grid
Maintain page objects and shared utilities
Integrate the suite with Maven, TestNG and CI
Investigate and fix flaky and failing tests

essential: Java (or another Selenium-supported language) with OOP

prerequisites: Java basics or willingness to learn Java first

beginner.title: Java and WebDriver basics
goals: Write Java programs using classes and collections
Explain how WebDriver communicates with browsers
Automate a form using robust locators

intermediate.title: Real-world UI handling
goals: Handle iframes, multiple windows and JavaScript alerts
Synchronise with dynamic content using explicit waits
Organise tests with TestNG groups and data providers

advanced.title: Scale the suite
goals: Run tests in parallel across browsers on a grid
Containerise the grid with Docker
Reduce flakiness with measured evidence

exercises: Automate a page with an embedded iframe and a popup window, switching contexts correctly
Set up Selenium Grid with Docker and run the same suite on Chrome and Firefox
Use TestNG data providers to drive a login test with valid and invalid credentials

sampleProject.title: Cross-browser Selenium framework
sampleProject.description: Create a Maven project using Selenium WebDriver, TestNG and page objects against a practice site. Include configuration for browser selection, a Docker Compose Selenium Grid, parallel execution, screenshots on failure, an HTML report and a Jenkins or GitHub Actions pipeline.

interviewQuestions.q: Describe the Selenium WebDriver architecture.
interviewQuestions.a: Test code uses a language binding to send commands defined by the W3C WebDriver protocol over HTTP to a browser-specific driver, such as chromedriver or geckodriver. The driver translates them into native browser actions and returns results. With Selenium Grid, commands go to a hub or router that forwards them to nodes running browsers.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you handle a StaleElementReferenceException?
interviewQuestions.a: It occurs when the element reference points to a DOM node that has been replaced, often after a re-render. I re-locate the element after the page updates, wait for the expected state rather than holding references for long, and keep element lookups inside page object methods. Blind retries hide the cause, so I use them sparingly.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you switch to an iframe and back?
interviewQuestions.a: I use driver.switchTo().frame() with an index, name or WebElement, ideally after waiting with frameToBeAvailableAndSwitchToIt. After working inside the frame I call switchTo().defaultContent() or parentFrame() to return. Forgetting to switch back is a common cause of NoSuchElementException.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you run tests in parallel with TestNG?
interviewQuestions.a: I configure parallel mode and thread count in testng.xml, for example parallel by methods or classes. Each thread must have its own WebDriver instance, typically managed with a ThreadLocal, and tests must not share mutable data. I also ensure test data is independent so tests can run in any order.

interviewQuestions.q: Why might XPath locators be problematic?
interviewQuestions.a: Absolute or deeply nested XPaths break when layout changes and are harder to read. XPath can be appropriate, for example to locate by text or to traverse to a parent, but I prefer IDs, test attributes or concise CSS selectors. The goal is locators tied to meaning, not structure.

roles.codingRequirements: Solid Java: OOP, collections, exceptions, generics basics; comfortable with Maven builds and reading stack traces.
commonMistakes: Mixing implicit and explicit waits
Sharing a single WebDriver across parallel threads
Not knowing what happens at the protocol level
readinessCriteria: You can explain the WebDriver protocol flow and Grid routing
You have run a suite in parallel on at least two browsers
You can handle frames, windows and alerts without looking up syntax
Your framework captures screenshots and logs on failure

roles.title: SDET (Software Development Engineer in Test)
roles.overview: An SDET is a software engineer whose product is testability and test infrastructure. SDETs write production-quality code for frameworks, tools and tests at all levels, review application code for testability, and design how testing fits into CI/CD. Interviews often resemble developer interviews, including coding problems and design questions.
responsibilities: Design and build test frameworks, utilities and test data tooling
Write unit, integration, API and UI tests alongside developers
Review application code and designs for testability
Integrate tests into CI/CD and keep pipelines fast and reliable
Use test doubles to isolate components and dependencies
Mentor team members on test design and automation practices

essential: Strong programming in Java, Python, C# or TypeScript
Framework design for UI and API testing
Test strategy and the test pyramid

prerequisites: Comfortable programming in at least one language
Understanding of testing fundamentals and test levels

beginner.title: Engineering foundations
goals: Solve common data-structure problems with arrays, maps and strings
Write unit tests with JUnit 5 or pytest
Apply OOP principles in test code
Use Git branches and pull requests

intermediate.title: Multi-level automation
goals: Build an API test layer with REST Assured or similar
Build a UI test layer with Playwright or Selenium
Use mocks and stubs to isolate dependencies
Apply design patterns such as builder and factory in tests

advanced.title: Testing as a platform
goals: Run the full suite in containers within a CI pipeline
Design a test architecture for a microservice system
Add contract tests between two services
Measure and reduce suite duration and flakiness

exercises: Solve ten easy and medium coding problems on strings, arrays and hash maps, with unit tests for each
Write unit tests with mocks for a service class that calls an external API
Design a framework with separate layers for configuration, clients, data builders and tests
Run API tests against a service started with Testcontainers in CI

sampleProject.title: Full-stack test platform for a sample service
sampleProject.description: Take a small open-source web service with a UI. Add unit tests with mocks, API tests with REST Assured or a Python HTTP client, a few Playwright end-to-end tests, and a contract test for one dependency. Run everything in GitHub Actions with Docker, publish reports, and document the architecture and test strategy.

interviewQuestions.q: How is an SDET different from an automation test engineer?
interviewQuestions.a: An automation engineer typically writes automated tests within an existing framework, mostly at UI and API level. An SDET is expected to design frameworks and tooling, work at every level including unit tests, contribute to application code testability, and own CI integration. The coding bar is closer to that of a software engineer.

interviewQuestions.q: Write a function to check whether a string is a palindrome, and how would you test it?
interviewQuestions.a: Use two pointers from the start and end moving inward, comparing characters, optionally normalising case and skipping non-alphanumerics according to the requirement. That is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Tests cover an empty string, a single character, even and odd lengths, mixed case, punctuation, and a non-palindrome differing only in the middle.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you design a test framework for a new product with web, API and mobile clients?
interviewQuestions.a: I would separate layers: configuration and environment handling, API clients, UI drivers per platform, shared test data builders, and the tests themselves. Shared business-level helpers sit above the clients so tests read in domain terms. Most coverage goes into fast API and component tests, with a thin set of end-to-end journeys per client, all running in CI with clear reporting.

interviewQuestions.q: When would you use a mock rather than a real dependency?
interviewQuestions.a: Use a mock when the dependency is slow, non-deterministic, costly or unavailable, or when you need to simulate errors that are hard to trigger. Use real dependencies, often in containers, when you need confidence in the actual integration. Too many mocks can make tests pass while real integration is broken, so I balance them with contract or integration tests.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you keep a large automated suite fast?
interviewQuestions.a: Push tests down the pyramid, run independent tests in parallel, reuse expensive setup carefully, and create data through APIs rather than the UI. Split pipelines so fast checks run on every commit and slower suites run on merge or nightly. I measure duration per test and treat slow tests as defects.

interviewQuestions.q: What makes test code maintainable?
interviewQuestions.a: Clear names that describe behaviour, no duplication of setup or locators, tests independent of each other, meaningful assertions with good failure messages, and abstraction layers that hide mechanics. It should be reviewed and refactored like production code.

roles.codingRequirements: Strong: production-quality code in Java, Python, C# or TypeScript; data structures and algorithms at a typical developer-interview level; OOP and design patterns.
commonMistakes: Underpreparing for coding questions because the title includes 'test'
Describing only UI automation and ignoring unit and API levels
Not testing your own solution during a coding exercise
Overusing mocks without discussing integration risk
readinessCriteria: You can solve typical easy and medium coding problems in 30 minutes, including tests
You have built a framework with both API and UI layers running in CI
You can explain your framework architecture and its trade-offs on a whiteboard
You have written unit tests with mocks for real code

roles.title: Test Automation Developer
roles.overview: A Test Automation Developer focuses on writing high-quality automated test code at scale, often in teams with a dedicated framework owned by others. The emphasis is on clean, reviewable code, broad coverage of product features and fast turnaround as features ship. It sits between an automation engineer and an SDET in coding depth.
responsibilities: Translate test cases and acceptance criteria into automated tests
Write clean, reviewed test code following team conventions
Extend shared helpers and page objects when needed
Create and manage test data programmatically
Keep automated tests up to date with product changes
Participate in code reviews of test and application code

roleSpecific: Writing readable assertions and failure messages
Working within an existing framework's conventions
optional: Static analysis and linting for test code

beginner.title: Code and tests
goals: Write automated tests that follow a consistent structure
Use Git branches, commits and pull requests confidently
Use a test runner's assertions and fixtures

intermediate.title: Productive in a framework
goals: Add tests to an existing page object framework
Generate test data through APIs
Refactor duplicated test code into helpers

advanced.title: Quality of test code
goals: Review peers' test code with actionable comments
Improve failure diagnostics with logs and reports
Reduce flakiness in owned tests

tools: REST Assured or a similar HTTP client
exercises: Refactor a messy 300-line test file into readable, reusable tests
Replace UI-based test setup with API-based data creation and measure the time saved
Review a sample pull request of test code and write five review comments

sampleProject.title: Refactoring a legacy test suite
sampleProject.description: Start from a deliberately messy automation suite (write one or take a small open-source example). Refactor it into clean page objects and helpers, move data setup to API calls, improve assertion messages, and document before and after metrics you actually measured, such as run time and lines of duplicated code.

interviewQuestions.q: What makes a good automated test?
interviewQuestions.a: It tests one behaviour, has a descriptive name, sets up its own data, is independent of other tests and of execution order, and has assertions that explain what went wrong when they fail. It should be deterministic and as fast as possible for its level.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you create test data for UI tests efficiently?
interviewQuestions.a: I create data through APIs or database seeding rather than clicking through the UI, which is faster and more reliable. Each test creates uniquely identified data so parallel runs do not collide, and cleans up where needed. The UI is then only used for the behaviour under test.

interviewQuestions.q: What do you look for when reviewing test code?
interviewQuestions.a: Whether the test actually verifies the intended behaviour, whether assertions are meaningful, duplication that should be extracted, hard-coded waits or data, and readability. I also check it follows framework conventions and fails with a useful message.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you write a helpful assertion failure message?
interviewQuestions.a: Include what was expected, what was observed and the relevant context such as the record ID or step. Libraries like AssertJ or Hamcrest produce descriptive messages by default and allow custom descriptions. A good message often lets you diagnose without rerunning.

roles.codingRequirements: Proficient in one language with clean code practices; comfortable with code review and refactoring.
commonMistakes: Writing tests that depend on each other's data
Not mentioning code review as part of quality
Treating test code as second-class code
readinessCriteria: You can add a new automated test to an unfamiliar framework by following its conventions
You have refactored test code and can show before and after
You create test data via API rather than UI where possible

roles.title: Test Framework Engineer
roles.overview: A Test Framework Engineer builds and evolves the internal libraries, conventions and tooling that other engineers use to write tests. The users of their work are other testers and developers, so API design, documentation, backwards compatibility and developer experience matter as much as test logic. It is a deeply technical role suited to people who enjoy building tools.
responsibilities: Design and maintain the core automation framework and its extension points
Provide configuration, reporting, logging and retry mechanisms
Integrate the framework with CI, test management and reporting tools
Write documentation, examples and migration guides for framework users
Manage versions, dependencies and breaking changes
Support teams adopting the framework and gather feedback

essential: Deep knowledge of at least one test runner
roleSpecific: Plugin and extension design for test runners

prerequisites: Experience writing automated tests in a framework
Strong command of one programming language

beginner.title: Understand frameworks
goals: Read and explain the structure of an existing framework
Use test runner lifecycle hooks and fixtures
Manage dependencies with Maven or npm

intermediate.title: Build reusable parts
goals: Implement configuration management for multiple environments
Add reporting and logging with screenshots and traces
Apply factory, builder and strategy patterns

advanced.title: Framework as a product
goals: Version and release the framework as a library
Add built-in flakiness detection and quarantine support
Integrate with CI and publish results centrally

exercises: Write a JUnit 5 extension or pytest plugin that captures a screenshot on failure
Implement environment configuration loading with overrides from environment variables
Write a migration guide for a breaking change in a framework API

sampleProject.title: Reusable automation library
sampleProject.description: Build a small framework library that provides driver management, configuration, reporting hooks and a page component base class. Publish it as a versioned package in a local registry or repository, write a separate example test project that consumes it, and document the public API and extension points.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you design configuration for a framework used across several environments?
interviewQuestions.a: I would use layered configuration: defaults in the repository, environment-specific files, and overrides from environment variables or CI parameters, with secrets coming only from a secret store. Configuration should be validated at start-up with clear errors. Tests should never hard-code URLs or credentials.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you introduce a breaking change in a shared framework?
interviewQuestions.a: I version the framework semantically, deprecate the old API first with warnings and documentation, and provide a migration guide and ideally an automated fix. I communicate timelines to consuming teams and remove the old API in a later major version. Monitoring usage helps decide when it is safe.

interviewQuestions.q: Which design patterns are useful in test frameworks?
interviewQuestions.a: Page Object and component objects for UI structure, Builder for test data, Factory for creating drivers or clients per configuration, Strategy for swapping behaviours like waiting or reporting, and Singleton only sparingly, since global state hurts parallel execution. Patterns should reduce complexity, not add it.

interviewQuestions.q: Should a framework retry failed tests automatically?
interviewQuestions.a: Retries can reduce noise from known infrastructure issues, but they also hide real intermittent defects. If I add retries, they are limited, visible in reports, and failing-then-passing tests are tracked as flaky so they get fixed. Retry should never be the default answer to instability.

roles.codingRequirements: Strong programming and software design skills, including API design, packaging and dependency management.
commonMistakes: Designing for features rather than for the people who will use the framework
Ignoring documentation and versioning
Treating automatic retries as a fix for flakiness
readinessCriteria: You have built a reusable library consumed by a separate test project
You can explain your framework's extension points and configuration model
You have written a runner extension or plugin

roles.title: QA Software Developer
roles.overview: A QA Software Developer builds software that supports testing: internal tools, simulators, test data generators, dashboards and harnesses, as well as automated tests. The role is closer to general software development than most testing roles, with the product's quality as its purpose. It suits developers who enjoy quality engineering problems.
responsibilities: Build internal tools for test data generation, environment setup and reporting
Develop simulators and stub services for dependencies
Write automated tests across levels
Maintain test-related services and their deployment
Collaborate with product developers on testability hooks
Document and support tools used by the QA team

essential: General software development in at least one language

prerequisites: Software development experience or a strong programming background

beginner.title: Developer and tester basics
goals: Write a small HTTP API and test it
Query and seed a database with SQL
Understand the test pyramid

intermediate.title: Tools for testers
goals: Build a test data generator that respects business rules
Build a stub service that simulates error responses
Package tools in Docker

advanced.title: Platform contributions
goals: Automate environment provisioning for tests
Build a results dashboard from CI data
Design testability hooks with product developers

tools: A web framework such as FastAPI, Spring Boot or Express
exercises: Write a CLI that generates valid and invalid customer records for a given schema
Build a stub payment service with configurable delays and error codes
Build a small page that summarises test results from JUnit XML reports

sampleProject.title: Configurable dependency simulator
sampleProject.description: Build a containerised stub service that simulates an external partner API, with endpoints to configure responses, latency and error rates per test. Include its own unit tests, API documentation, and an example automated test suite that uses it to test a client application's error handling.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you build a test data generator?
interviewQuestions.a: I would model the domain rules explicitly, then generate data that satisfies them, plus deliberate invalid variants for negative tests. Generators should be deterministic when seeded so failures can be reproduced. I would create data through public APIs where possible so it is valid in the same way real data is.

interviewQuestions.q: Why build a simulator rather than use the real dependency in tests?
interviewQuestions.a: A simulator gives control over responses, latency and failures, works offline, and avoids costs or rate limits of the real service. It enables testing of error paths that are difficult to trigger for real. It must be kept aligned with the real contract, which contract tests or periodic checks can verify.

interviewQuestions.q: What testability hooks would you ask product developers for?
interviewQuestions.a: Stable test identifiers in the UI, ways to set time or feature flags in test environments, endpoints or scripts to seed and reset data, and correlation IDs in logs. These must be disabled or protected in production. They dramatically reduce test complexity and flakiness.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you test your own internal tools?
interviewQuestions.a: The same way as product code: unit tests for logic, integration tests for I/O, and CI on every change. Tools used by many testers become critical infrastructure, and a broken tool can mislead the whole team.

roles.codingRequirements: Strong general development skills: building services and CLIs, databases, testing your own code.
commonMistakes: Not testing the tools you build
Building tools without understanding testers' actual workflow
Leaving testability hooks unprotected in production
readinessCriteria: You have built and deployed at least one service with its own tests
You can design a simulator for an external API including failure modes
You can generate rule-compliant test data programmatically

roles.title: Web Automation Engineer
roles.overview: A Web Automation Engineer focuses on automating modern web front ends, often single-page applications, using tools such as Playwright, Cypress or WebdriverIO, usually in TypeScript. The role requires understanding of the DOM, browser events, network behaviour and front-end frameworks so tests are fast and stable. It often works closely with front-end developers.
responsibilities: Automate end-to-end and component-level tests for web applications
Use network interception to control and verify API traffic
Run tests across browser engines and viewports
Add automated accessibility and visual checks where valuable
Maintain fixtures, test data and authentication state
Integrate tests into front-end CI pipelines

essential: A modern web automation tool (Playwright, Cypress or WebdriverIO)
DOM, CSS selectors and accessible locators

beginner.title: Web fundamentals
goals: Write TypeScript functions using async and await
Locate elements by role, label and test ID
Automate a form in Playwright or Cypress

intermediate.title: Stable, fast web tests
goals: Mock and assert on network calls
Reuse authenticated state across tests
Structure tests with fixtures and page objects

advanced.title: Broader quality signals
goals: Add automated accessibility scanning
Run tests in parallel and sharded in CI
Investigate failures using traces and videos

exercises: Write Playwright tests for a single-page app using only role-based locators
Mock an API response to test an empty state and an error state in the UI
Add an axe accessibility scan to three pages and triage findings

sampleProject.title: Playwright suite for a single-page application
sampleProject.description: Automate an open-source single-page app with Playwright and TypeScript: role-based locators, fixtures, reused authentication state, network mocking for error states, an accessibility scan, cross-browser projects, and a sharded GitHub Actions workflow that uploads traces on failure.

interviewQuestions.q: How does Playwright's auto-waiting work?
interviewQuestions.a: Before performing an action, Playwright checks actionability conditions such as the element being attached, visible, stable, enabled and receiving events, retrying until a timeout. Web-first assertions like toBeVisible also retry. This removes most manual waits, though you still need to wait on the right condition, such as a network response, in some cases.

interviewQuestions.q: Why prefer role-based locators?
interviewQuestions.a: Locators like getByRole with an accessible name reflect how users and assistive technology perceive the page, so they are resilient to markup and styling changes. They also encourage accessible markup. Test IDs remain a good fallback where no meaningful role or name exists.

interviewQuestions.q: When would you mock network responses in an end-to-end test?
interviewQuestions.a: When I need to test UI behaviour for states that are hard to produce for real, such as server errors, empty results or slow responses, or to isolate the front end from an unstable backend. I keep some unmocked journeys so the real integration is also covered.

interviewQuestions.q: How is Cypress architecturally different from Selenium?
interviewQuestions.a: Cypress runs test code inside the browser alongside the application, giving direct access to the DOM and network with automatic waiting. Selenium drives the browser externally via the WebDriver protocol. Cypress historically had restrictions around multiple tabs and cross-origin navigation; its support has changed across versions, so checking current documentation matters.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you debug a failure that only happens in CI?
interviewQuestions.a: I enable trace or video capture on failure and inspect the trace for the DOM snapshot, network calls and console at the failing step. I check differences like viewport, headless mode, fonts, timezone and test data. Reproducing with the same container image locally often makes the cause obvious.

roles.codingRequirements: Solid JavaScript or TypeScript including async/await and promises; basic HTML, CSS and DOM knowledge.
commonMistakes: Using CSS class selectors tied to styling frameworks
Mocking every network call so the real integration is never tested
Adding fixed timeouts instead of waiting on conditions
readinessCriteria: You can automate a new page using accessible locators without fixed waits
You have used network interception to test at least two error states
Your suite runs in parallel in CI and produces traces on failure

roles.title: API Automation Engineer
roles.overview: An API Automation Engineer builds automated test suites for HTTP APIs, which are faster and more stable than UI tests and catch business logic defects early. The role requires solid HTTP knowledge, a programming language and libraries such as REST Assured, plus skill at chaining requests, validating schemas and managing test data. It is a high-value role in service-oriented systems.
responsibilities: Design automated tests for API endpoints covering functional, negative and boundary cases
Validate status codes, headers, bodies and JSON schemas
Automate authentication flows and token handling
Manage test data creation and clean-up via APIs
Run API suites in CI on every change
Verify API results against the database where appropriate

essential: HTTP methods, status codes and headers
One programming language with an HTTP test library
Authentication schemes such as tokens and OAuth flows
roleSpecific: Request chaining and test data management
Testing pagination, idempotency and rate limiting

beginner.title: HTTP and first API tests
goals: Explain HTTP methods, status codes and headers
Build a Postman collection with tests
Read and write JSON confidently

intermediate.title: Code-based API suites
goals: Write REST Assured or Python tests with reusable request specifications
Validate responses with JSON Schema
Automate token-based authentication

advanced.title: Robust API quality
goals: Test pagination, idempotency and rate limits
Add contract tests for a consumer
Run API tests in CI with environment configuration

exercises: Write a REST Assured suite for a public practice API covering CRUD and error cases
Validate every response against a JSON Schema and break the schema to see failures
Automate an authentication flow and reuse the token across tests

sampleProject.title: API test suite with schema validation
sampleProject.description: Build an API test project for a locally run open-source REST service using REST Assured or pytest. Cover CRUD, authentication, validation errors, pagination and idempotency, validate schemas, create and clean up data through the API, and run everything in CI with environment-based configuration.

interviewQuestions.q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
interviewQuestions.a: PUT replaces the target resource with the representation sent, so omitted fields may be removed or reset, and it is defined as idempotent. PATCH applies a partial modification and is not guaranteed to be idempotent. Tests should verify the API behaves according to its documented semantics for each.

interviewQuestions.q: What would you test for a POST /orders endpoint?
interviewQuestions.a: Valid creation returns 201 with the created resource and a location or ID; required fields missing or wrong types return 400 with useful errors; unauthenticated requests return 401 and unauthorised ones 403. I would test boundary values, duplicates and idempotency keys if supported, and verify the order was persisted correctly. I would also check the response schema and that no sensitive data leaks.

interviewQuestions.q: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
interviewQuestions.a: 401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid authentication credentials. 403 Forbidden means the server understood who the client is but refuses access to that resource. Testing both for each protected endpoint catches many authorisation defects.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you manage test data in API automation?
interviewQuestions.a: Each test creates the data it needs through the API with unique identifiers, uses it, and cleans up where the system allows. Shared reference data is seeded once and treated as read-only. This makes tests independent and safe to run in parallel.

interviewQuestions.q: Why validate JSON schemas in addition to field assertions?
interviewQuestions.a: Schema validation checks the structure of the whole response: required fields, types and formats, catching unexpected changes in fields you did not explicitly assert on. Field assertions check specific business values. Together they catch both contract drift and logic errors.

roles.codingRequirements: Moderate: one language (Java with REST Assured, Python with pytest, or JavaScript) including working with JSON, collections and HTTP clients.
commonMistakes: Only checking status codes, not bodies and side effects
Confusing 401 with 403
Making tests depend on data created by previous tests
readinessCriteria: You can design tests for any CRUD endpoint covering positive, negative and authorisation cases
You have a code-based API suite with schema validation running in CI
You can explain HTTP method semantics and idempotency accurately

roles.title: Mobile Automation Engineer
roles.overview: A Mobile Automation Engineer automates tests for Android and iOS applications, commonly with Appium or native frameworks such as Espresso and XCUITest. Mobile brings extra challenges: device fragmentation, gestures, permissions, app lifecycle and slower, more variable execution. The role blends automation skill with solid mobile platform knowledge.
responsibilities: Automate functional tests for native, hybrid or mobile web apps
Manage emulators, simulators and real devices for test execution
Handle gestures, permissions, notifications and app lifecycle events
Choose device and OS coverage for automated runs
Integrate mobile tests into CI, including device clouds where used
Investigate platform-specific failures

essential: One programming language (Java, Kotlin, Swift, Python or JavaScript)
roleSpecific: Emulator, simulator and real device management
App lifecycle, permissions and interruption testing

prerequisites: Experience using Android and iOS devices

beginner.title: Mobile basics
goals: Explain differences between native, hybrid and mobile web apps
Set up Appium with an Android emulator
Locate elements with the Appium Inspector

intermediate.title: Real-world mobile automation
goals: Automate gestures such as swipe, scroll and long press
Handle permission dialogs and app backgrounding
Apply page objects to mobile screens

advanced.title: Scale across devices
goals: Define a device and OS coverage matrix
Run tests in parallel on several devices in CI
Reduce flakiness specific to mobile

exercises: Automate login and a list scroll in a sample Android app with Appium
Test app behaviour when a permission is denied and later granted
Write a device coverage matrix for a consumer app and justify each choice

sampleProject.title: Cross-platform Appium suite
sampleProject.description: Automate an open-source mobile app on Android (and iOS if you have macOS) with Appium and page objects. Cover login, navigation, gestures, a permission prompt and backgrounding. Run on emulators in CI, document capabilities and setup, and include a device coverage rationale.

interviewQuestions.q: Explain the Appium architecture.
interviewQuestions.a: Appium is a server that implements the WebDriver protocol. Client libraries send commands to the Appium server, which routes them to a platform driver, such as UiAutomator2 for Android or XCUITest for iOS, which in turn uses the platform's native automation framework. In Appium 2, drivers are installed separately as plugins to the server.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you decide which devices to test on?
interviewQuestions.a: I use the product's own usage analytics where available to choose OS versions, screen sizes and manufacturers that cover most users, plus important edge cases like the minimum supported OS. Emulators handle broad coverage cheaply, while real devices cover hardware-specific behaviour. The matrix is reviewed as usage changes.

interviewQuestions.q: What mobile-specific scenarios would you test?
interviewQuestions.a: Interruptions such as calls and notifications, backgrounding and resuming, rotation, network changes including offline, permissions granted and denied, low storage and battery, and app upgrades preserving data. These rarely exist on the web but often cause mobile defects.

interviewQuestions.q: When would you choose Espresso or XCUITest over Appium?
interviewQuestions.a: Native frameworks run closer to the app, are typically faster and more stable, and integrate with the developers' build, which suits teams where developers co-own tests. Appium suits cross-platform suites with one codebase and teams testing apps as black boxes. Many organisations use both at different levels.

interviewQuestions.q: Why are mobile tests often flakier than web tests?
interviewQuestions.a: Devices and emulators vary in speed, animations and system dialogs appear unpredictably, and network conditions fluctuate. Mitigations include disabling animations on test devices, waiting on explicit conditions, resetting app state between tests and keeping device setups consistent.

roles.codingRequirements: Working proficiency in one language used with Appium or native frameworks; Kotlin or Swift needed for native frameworks.
commonMistakes: Assuming emulators reproduce all real-device behaviour
Ignoring interruptions and app lifecycle
Not knowing the difference between Appium 1 and Appium 2 driver model
readinessCriteria: You have an Appium suite running on at least one emulator in CI
You can automate common gestures and permission prompts
You can justify a device coverage matrix

roles.title: Test Infrastructure Engineer
roles.overview: A Test Infrastructure Engineer builds and runs the systems that execute tests: CI pipelines, browser and device grids, ephemeral environments, test data services and results storage. The role overlaps heavily with DevOps but is focused on making testing fast, reliable and observable at scale. Strong scripting, containers and CI skills matter more than UI automation.
responsibilities: Design and maintain CI pipelines that run test suites efficiently
Provision ephemeral test environments with containers
Operate browser grids and device infrastructure
Implement test sharding, parallelism and caching
Collect, store and visualise test results and flakiness data
Manage secrets and configuration for test environments safely

essential: CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions or Jenkins
Understanding of test suites and their needs
roleSpecific: Test result analytics and flakiness tracking
optional: Infrastructure as code such as Terraform

beginner.title: CI and containers
goals: Write a CI workflow that builds and tests a project
Run an application and its database in Docker Compose
Use Git branching with CI triggers

intermediate.title: Fast pipelines
goals: Shard a test suite across parallel jobs
Cache dependencies to reduce pipeline time
Run a Selenium or Playwright grid in containers

advanced.title: Observable test platform
goals: Track flaky tests automatically across runs
Provision per-pull-request environments
Report pipeline health metrics

exercises: Shard a Playwright or pytest suite across four CI jobs and merge the reports
Spin up an application, database and test runner in Docker Compose for each CI run
Write a script that parses JUnit XML from multiple runs and lists tests with inconsistent results

sampleProject.title: Ephemeral test environment pipeline
sampleProject.description: Build a CI pipeline that, for each pull request, starts an application stack in containers, seeds test data, runs API and UI tests in parallel shards, publishes merged reports, records results to a store, and tears everything down. Document timings you actually measured before and after optimisation.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you reduce a test pipeline from 60 minutes to 15?
interviewQuestions.a: First measure where time goes: setup, build, individual slow tests. Then parallelise or shard test execution, cache dependencies and build outputs, reuse container images, and move slow or low-value tests to a later stage. Often test-level fixes such as API-based setup give big gains too.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you detect flaky tests systematically?
interviewQuestions.a: Store results per test across runs and flag tests that both pass and fail on the same commit, or that pass on retry. Report a flakiness rate and owners, and quarantine visibly while fixes happen. Without historical data, flakiness is just anecdote.

interviewQuestions.q: How should secrets be handled in test pipelines?
interviewQuestions.a: Secrets come from the CI system's secret store or a vault, are scoped to the jobs that need them, and are never committed or printed in logs. Test environments use separate credentials from production with least privilege. Forked pull requests should not get access to secrets.

interviewQuestions.q: What are the benefits of ephemeral test environments?
interviewQuestions.a: Each run gets a clean, isolated environment, which removes interference between teams and stale data problems. Environments match the code under test exactly. The costs are provisioning time and infrastructure spend, so images and seeding need to be fast.

roles.codingRequirements: Strong scripting (Bash, Python) and CI configuration; comfortable with containers and Linux.
commonMistakes: Optimising without measuring first
Treating retries as the solution to flakiness
Exposing secrets in logs or to untrusted pull requests
readinessCriteria: You have built a CI pipeline that runs tests in parallel shards
You can stand up an application stack in containers for testing
You have a script or dashboard that reports flaky tests from real run data

roles.title: Test Architect
roles.overview: A Test Architect defines how testing is structured across a product or organisation: which levels and types of testing exist, where they run, which tools are standard, and how quality signals flow into delivery decisions. The role is senior and technical, balancing hands-on prototyping with strategy and influence. Decisions are about trade-offs, not single tools.
responsibilities: Define test strategy and architecture across teams and systems
Select and standardise tools and frameworks with documented trade-offs
Design test approaches for complex systems such as microservices
Guide teams on testability in system and service design
Define quality gates and metrics in CI/CD
Mentor engineers and review test designs

essential: Broad automation experience across UI, API and unit levels
Test strategy and the test pyramid
System design and distributed systems basics
roleSpecific: Contract and integration test strategy for services

prerequisites: Several years of hands-on automation or SDET experience
Experience across more than one product or system

beginner.title: Strategic foundations
goals: Write a test strategy for a single product
Map existing tests onto the test pyramid and find gaps
Document a tool choice with alternatives and trade-offs

intermediate.title: Architect for systems
goals: Design testing for a microservice system with contract tests
Define environment and test data strategy
Design CI quality gates

advanced.title: Organisation-wide quality
goals: Define metrics that show the effectiveness of testing
Integrate performance and security testing into the strategy
Lead adoption across multiple teams

tools: CI platforms such as GitHub Actions or Jenkins
exercises: Write a test strategy for a system of five microservices and a web front end
Write an architecture decision record comparing two UI automation tools for your context
Design CI quality gates and explain what failures block a release

sampleProject.title: Test architecture for a microservice demo
sampleProject.description: Choose an open-source microservice demo application. Produce a test architecture document with diagrams covering levels, ownership, contract tests, environments, data strategy and CI gates, and implement a vertical slice: unit, contract, API and one end-to-end test running in a pipeline.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you design the test strategy for a system of many microservices?
interviewQuestions.a: Most confidence should come from fast unit and component tests within each service, plus consumer-driven contract tests between services so teams can deploy independently. A small number of end-to-end tests cover critical journeys in an integrated environment, complemented by monitoring in production. I would define ownership, environments and CI gates for each level.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you evaluate a new testing tool?
interviewQuestions.a: I define criteria from our context: languages, application technology, team skills, maintenance cost, CI integration, licensing and community health. I run a time-boxed proof of concept on a real, difficult part of our product, then record the decision and the alternatives considered. Tool popularity alone is not a reason.

interviewQuestions.q: What is the risk of relying heavily on end-to-end tests?
interviewQuestions.a: They are slow, expensive to maintain and often flaky, and failures are hard to diagnose because many components are involved. Teams start ignoring red builds. They are valuable for critical journeys but should sit on top of strong lower-level coverage.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you know whether the test strategy is working?
interviewQuestions.a: Look at outcomes: escaped defects and their severity, where defects are found, lead time and pipeline duration, and flakiness rates. Trends matter more than absolute values. I also gather qualitative feedback from teams about confidence and friction.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you get teams to adopt a new standard?
interviewQuestions.a: Involve them in the decision, demonstrate value on a real problem, provide templates, documentation and support, and migrate incrementally. Mandates without support tend to fail. I measure adoption and address blockers openly.

roles.codingRequirements: Strong: able to prototype frameworks and review code at a senior engineering level, though day-to-day work is more design than coding.
commonMistakes: Answering with one favourite tool for every context
Ignoring organisational and people factors
No measurable way to judge whether the strategy works
readinessCriteria: You have written and defended a test strategy for a multi-component system
You have led at least one tool evaluation with a documented decision
You can explain trade-offs of contract versus end-to-end testing clearly

roles.title: QA Technical Lead
roles.overview: A QA Technical Lead guides the technical direction of testing within a team or group of teams while remaining hands-on. They set coding and design standards for test code, unblock engineers, review pull requests and coordinate automation priorities with delivery leads. The role combines strong automation skills with mentoring and planning.
responsibilities: Set technical standards and review test code across the team
Plan automation work and align it with release priorities
Mentor testers and automation engineers
Lead investigations into difficult failures and flaky suites
Represent QA in technical design discussions
Report automation health and quality risks to delivery leads

essential: Clear communication with engineering and product

prerequisites: Several years as an automation engineer or SDET

beginner.title: Lead by example
goals: Write review guidelines for test code
Mentor one junior engineer on framework usage
Own the health of the team's CI suite

intermediate.title: Plan and coordinate
goals: Estimate and plan automation for a release
Prioritise automation backlog by risk and value
Report automation health metrics

advanced.title: Technical leadership
goals: Drive a framework or tooling improvement across teams
Contribute testability input to system designs
Coach the team through a change in practice

tools: The team's automation stack (for example Playwright, Selenium or REST Assured)
exercises: Write a one-page code review checklist for automated tests
Plan automation for a release with ten stories and justify priorities
Prepare a 30-minute knowledge-sharing session on a framework feature

sampleProject.title: Automation health improvement plan
sampleProject.description: For an existing open-source or personal automation suite, measure current duration, failure and flakiness rates, write a prioritised improvement plan with owners and milestones, implement the top two improvements, and present the measured results and lessons as a short write-up.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you balance hands-on work with leading the team?
interviewQuestions.a: I keep hands-on work to tasks that are not on the critical path, such as framework improvements or investigations, so I do not block others when I am in meetings. My priority is unblocking people and reviewing work quickly. I reassess the balance as the team grows.

interviewQuestions.q: A junior engineer keeps submitting flaky tests. How do you handle it?
interviewQuestions.a: I pair with them on one example to understand the root cause, whether it is synchronisation, test data or design. Then I share a short guide with patterns to follow and add review checks for the common mistakes. The aim is to build their skill, not just fix the tests.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you prioritise an automation backlog?
interviewQuestions.a: By risk and return: critical business flows, frequently run regression areas and tests that block releases come first. I also weigh maintenance cost and whether the check belongs at a lower level. Priorities are reviewed with the product and delivery leads.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you report automation health to management?
interviewQuestions.a: With a few trends: pass rate excluding known issues, flaky test count, suite duration, and coverage of critical journeys. I explain what the numbers mean for release confidence and what actions we are taking. I avoid vanity metrics such as raw test counts.

roles.codingRequirements: Strong: senior-level coding in the team's automation language and the ability to review and refactor others' code.
commonMistakes: Talking only about personal technical work and not about the team
Using test count as the main success metric
No examples of mentoring or resolving disagreements
readinessCriteria: You have mentored at least one engineer and can describe the outcome
You have planned automation work for a release and tracked delivery
You can present automation health with meaningful metrics
